title: Is Model Instability just Noise to be Tolerated or a Property that can be Managed?

edges.target: EZR default configuration (Menzies & Srinivasan)
edges.ref: [52] T. Menzies and S. Srinivasan, "Can AI be easy? Lessons learned from the ezr.py toolkit," 2026.
edges.evidence: Throughout the results, we compare two EZR configurations: initial (the defaults of [52]) and refined (Table IV).

edges.target: KMeans clustering (MacQueen)
edges.ref: [44] J. MacQueen, "Some methods for classification and analysis of multivariate observations," Proc. 5th Berkeley Symposium, 1967.
edges.evidence: RQ3 also runs three clusterers (KMeans, HDBSCAN, CURE; rationale in §II-C) as stability anchors.

edges.target: HDBSCAN (Campello et al.)
edges.ref: [45] R. J. G. B. Campello, D. Moulavi, and J. Sander, "Density-based clustering based on hierarchical density estimates," PAKDD 2013.
edges.evidence: we evaluate one method from each major family: KMeans [44] ..., HDBSCAN [45] (density-based clustering ...), and CURE [46]

edges.target: CURE clustering (Guha et al.)
edges.ref: [46] S. Guha, R. Rastogi, and K. Shim, "Cure: An efficient clustering algorithm for large databases," ACM SIGMOD Record, 1998.
edges.evidence: Comparing Performance and stability of EZR with clustering methods. Green bars and red lines show the stability and performance scores across 127 datasets.

edges.target: Cliff's delta effect size (Rosenthal; Sawilowsky; Macbeth et al.)
edges.ref: [60] Rosenthal et al. 1994; [61] Sawilowsky 2009; [62] Macbeth et al., "Cliff's delta calculator," Universitas Psychologica 2011.
edges.evidence: A K-S test [59] at α = 0.05 plus Cliff's delta δ ≤ 0.195 (small-to-medium) [60]–[62].

edges.target: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (Lilliefors)
edges.ref: [59] H. W. Lilliefors, "On the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for normality with mean and variance unknown," JASA, 1967.
edges.evidence: A K-S test [59] at α = 0.05 plus Cliff's delta δ ≤ 0.195

edges.target: Effect-size guidance for SE experiments (Kampenes et al.)
edges.ref: [58] V. B. Kampenes, T. Dybå, J. E. Hannay, D. I. Sjøberg, "A systematic review of effect size in software engineering experiments," IST 2007.
edges.evidence: we require statistical significance and practical effect size, avoiding p-value-only pitfalls [58].

edges.target: Top-set ranking via variance-maximizing iterative partition (Scott-Knott style)
edges.ref: [30] L. Semenova, H. Chen, R. Parr, C. Rudin, "A path to simpler models starts with noise," NeurIPS 2023. (citation as printed; likely mis-cited)
edges.evidence: To rank many treatments we find the top set: a variance-maximizing iterative partition [30] peels away distinguishably worse treatments

edges.target: Weighted Jaccard feature-stability measure (Kalousis et al.)
edges.ref: [57] A. Kalousis, J. Prados, M. Hilario, "Stability of feature selection algorithms: a study on high-dimensional spaces," KAIS 2007.
edges.evidence: Following Kalousis et al. [57], we use Jaccard similarity to compare the structure of two trees trained under identical settings.

edges.target: PromiseTune confounder filter (Chen & Chen)
edges.ref: [50] P. Chen and T. Chen, "Promisetune: Unveiling causally promising and explainable configuration tuning," 2025.
edges.evidence: Following PromiseTune, we add a confounder filter to our model construction.

edges.target: Gain-ratio splitting criterion for stable trees (Lee et al.)
edges.ref: [51] J. Lee, M. K. Sim, J.-S. Hong, "Assessing decision tree stability: a comprehensive method for generating a stable decision tree," IEEE Access 2024.
edges.evidence: After filtering, splits are scored by the gain ratio 1−H(Y|X)/H(Y), the most stable splitting criterion per Lee et al. [51].

edges.target: MOOT repository (Chen & Menzies)
edges.ref: [43] T. Menzies, T. Chen, Y. Ye, K. K. Ganguly, A. Rayegan, S. Srinivasan, A. Lustosa, "Moot: a repository of many multi-objective optimization tasks," MSR 2026.
edges.evidence: We use 127 multi-objective SE optimization problems from Chen & Menzies' MOOT repository http://tiny.cc/moot [43].

edges.target: 150-label saturation result (Menzies & Srinivasan)
edges.ref: [52] T. Menzies and S. Srinivasan, "Can AI be easy? Lessons learned from the ezr.py toolkit," 2026.
edges.evidence: This is consistent with (indeed, slightly more generous than) the 150-label saturation effect reported by Menzies and Srinivasan [52]

edges.target: Rashomon ratio / label-noise theory (Semenova, Rudin, Xin et al.)
edges.ref: [28] Semenova, Rudin, Parr, FAccT 2022; [30] Semenova et al., NeurIPS 2023; [14] Xin et al., NeurIPS 2022; [29] Rudin et al., arXiv:2407.04846, 2024.
edges.evidence: Semenova et al. [30] explain why Rashomon ratios tend to be large. Label noise widens generalization gaps and forces simpler model classes with greater multiplicity.
edges.section: II-B Structural Instability and the Rashomon Effect

edges.target: Breiman's instability/stabilization heuristics
edges.ref: [63] L. Breiman, "Heuristics of instability and stabilization in model selection," Annals of Statistics, 1996.
edges.evidence: by replacing trees with stable-by-design clusterers [63] that model local regions rather than a single global structure.

edges.target: EZR active-learning optimizer (ezr.py)
edges.ref: [53] T. Menzies, "The case for compact AI," CACM 2025; [52] Menzies & Srinivasan, "Can AI be easy? Lessons learned from the ezr.py toolkit," 2026.
edges.evidence: Our primary learner is EZR [53], the active-learning optimizer shown in Figure 4.

edges.target: Seed-varied EZR trees on Coc1000 (Rayegan & Menzies causality paper)
edges.ref: [12] A. Rayegan and T. Menzies, "Can causality cure confusion caused by correlation (in software analytics)?" arXiv:2602.16091, 2026.
edges.evidence: Results are from 4 repeats varying only the random seed, extracted from [12], on Coc1000 dataset from MOOT

edges.target: LDA topic instability measurements (Agrawal, Fu & Menzies)
edges.ref: [8] A. Agrawal, W. Fu, and T. Menzies, "What is wrong with topic modeling? and how to fix it using search-based software engineering," IST 2018.
edges.evidence: Running LDA twice with different orderings (Table I), only 3 of 40 topics recurred, and over half (25 of 40) had 55% or less overlap.

edges.target: Regression coefficient instability in effort estimation (Menzies et al.)
edges.ref: [7] T. Menzies, A. Butcher, D. Cok, A. Marcus, L. Layman, F. Shull, B. Turhan, T. Zimmermann, "Local versus global lessons for defect prediction and effort estimation," TSE 2012.
edges.evidence: Figure 3, from Menzies et al. [7], shows the βi learned from 20 different 66% samples of the same project dataset. The coefficients swing wildly, and half a dozen even cross βi = 0.

edges.target: Time-based conclusion instability in CPDP (Bangash et al.)
edges.ref: [9] A. A. Bangash, H. Sahar, A. Hindle, K. Ali, "On the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction models," EMSE 2020.
edges.evidence: Across five cross-project defect prediction techniques and 33 versions of 14 Java projects, rankings and performance shifted by statistically significant margins in time-aware evaluations

edges.target: Causal-graph structural instability measurements (Hulse, Eisty & Menzies)
edges.ref: [10] J. Hulse, N. U. Eisty, and T. Menzies, "Shaky structures: The wobbly world of causal graphs in software analytics," EMSE 2025.
edges.evidence: over half the causal edges disappeared or changed direction. Around 75% of edges differ between consecutive project releases, and removing just 10% of training data can cause large structural changes.

edges.target: LLM prompting instability in vulnerability detection (Han et al.)
edges.ref: [23] S. Han, T. Tan, Y. Miao, X. Chen, N. Sun, "Prompting instability: An empirical study of LLM robustness in code vulnerability detection," AJCAI 2025.
edges.evidence: Han et al. [23] tested 6 LLMs on 48 scenarios drawn from the MITRE Top-25 weaknesses, across 17 prompt structures with 20 paraphrases each.

edges.target: 10^46 configuration-space size for text-mining preprocessing (Agrawal et al. DODGE)
edges.ref: [19] A. Agrawal, W. Fu, D. Chen, X. Shen, T. Menzies, "How to 'dodge' complex software analytics," TSE 2019.
edges.evidence: Table 1 of Agrawal et al. [19] reports one hundred sextillion (10^46) ways to configure text-preprocessing data miners.

edges.target: EZR up-to-500x speedup over SMAC3 (Lindauer et al.; Menzies group measurement)
edges.ref: [56] M. Lindauer et al., "SMAC3: A versatile Bayesian optimization package for hyperparameter optimization," JMLR 2022; number reported via [52],[34],[55].
edges.evidence: EZR learns decision trees from only a few dozen labeled examples while achieving state-of-the-art optimization performance and running up to 500× faster than methods such as SMAC3 [56].

edges.target: Rashomon effect as named concept (Breiman two cultures; Xin et al.)
edges.ref: [13] L. Breiman, "Statistical modeling: The two cultures," Statistical Science 2001; [14] R. Xin et al., "Exploring the whole Rashomon set of sparse decision trees," NeurIPS 2022.
edges.evidence: This is the Rashomon effect: an enormous number of structurally different models can fit the same data [13], [14].

edges.target: EZR state-of-the-art credentials (Rayegan & Menzies JSS; Ganguly & Menzies FSE/arXiv)
edges.ref: [34] A. Rayegan and T. Menzies, JSS 2026; [54] K. K. Ganguly and T. Menzies, FSE 2026; [55] K. Ganguly and T. Menzies, arXiv:2605.09658, 2026.
edges.evidence: Recent studies in 2026 by Rayegan et al. and Ganguly et al., published in JSS [34] and FSE [54], establish EZR as a state-of-the-art baseline in SE multiobjective optimization [55]

edges.target: Pearl's warning about correlation-only learners (Causality; Book of Why)
edges.ref: [47] J. Pearl, Causality, CUP 2009; [48] J. Pearl and D. Mackenzie, The Book of Why, Basic Books 2018.
edges.evidence: Pearl warns that learners built on raw correlation invent influences that do not exist [47], [48]

edges.target: Unicorn causal configuration-performance reasoning (Iqbal et al.)
edges.ref: [49] M. S. Iqbal, R. Krishna, M. A. Javidian, B. Ray, P. Jamshidi, "Unicorn: Reasoning about configurable system performance through the lens of causality," EuroSys 2022.
edges.evidence: Causal knowledge can steady a learner. Unicorn [49] uses causality to sharpen configuration models, and PromiseTune [50] filters spurious predictors before search.

edges.target: SE data are noisy and label-scarce (Wu et al.; Seiffert et al.; Nair FLASH; Rayegan & Menzies)
edges.ref: [31] Wu, Zheng, Xia, Lo, TSE 2021; [32] Seiffert et al., IRI 2007; [33] Nair, Yu, Menzies, Siegmund, Apel, TSE 2020; [34] Rayegan and Menzies, JSS 2026.
edges.evidence: SE datasets, often noisy [31], [32], small, and labeled under tight budgets [33], [34], are precisely those conditions.
edges.section: II-B Structural Instability and the Rashomon Effect

notes: Empirical study (127 MOOT tasks, 20 seeds); v1's three sanitycheck edges became numericfact/theory and the Fig.2 tree reuse became replication; v1's 'not-reuse' motivational numbers ([7],[8],[10],[23],[19], 500x SMAC3) are now numericfact edges; top-set ranking still cited as [30] (likely mis-citation of Scott-Knott); d2h and acquisition rules carry no prior-paper citation.
